title: Work, Energy, Power & Circular Loop
subtitle: Zero-to-JEE-Advanced Visual Textbook: Work by Variable Forces, Work-Energy Theorem, Conservative vs. Non-Conservative Forces, Potential Energy Curves, Springs & Vertical Circular Motion
introduction:
💡 First-Time Reader Intuition: What Is Energy?

In Chapter 04, we used Newton's Second Law ($\sum \vec{F} = m\vec{a}$) to analyze forces directly. While powerful, solving vector differential equations for complex paths can become extremely tedious.

The Energy Shortcut:
Energy is a scalar quantity (it has magnitude only, no direction!). By using the Work-Energy Theorem and Conservation of Mechanical Energy, we can bypass complex vector acceleration paths entirely and solve motion problems using simple arithmetic and algebra!

topics.title: Work Done by Constant & Variable Forces, Scalar Dot Product & The Work-Energy Theorem
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 Definition of Work Done
Definition:
Work is done by a force when it displaces an object. It is defined mathematically as the scalar (dot) product of the force vector $\vec{F}$ and the displacement vector $\vec{s}$.
$$\text{1. Constant Force:} \quad \boxed{W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{s} = Fs\cos\theta} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{2. Variable Force:} \quad \boxed{W = \int_{x_i}^{x_f} \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}}$$
  • Positive Work ($0^\circ \le \theta < 90^\circ$): Force assists motion (e.g., gravity pulling a falling object, tension accelerating a load).
  • Zero Work ($\theta = 90^\circ$): Force is perpendicular to displacement (e.g., centripetal force in uniform circular motion, normal force on a sliding block).
  • Negative Work ($90^\circ < \theta \le 180^\circ$): Force opposes motion (e.g., friction slowing down a car, gravity acting on an upward-thrown ball).
1.2 The Work-Energy Theorem (The Master Key of Mechanics)
Statement:
The net work done by all forces acting on a particle is always equal to the change in its kinetic energy ($K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$), regardless of whether the forces are conservative or non-conservative, constant or variable!
$$\boxed{W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = K_f - K_i = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{1}{2}mu^2}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of the Work-Energy Theorem

Start with Newton's Second Law $F_{\text{net}} = m\frac{dv}{dt}$. Multiply both sides by displacement $dx$ ($v = dx/dt$):

$$F_{\text{net}} \, dx = m \left(\frac{dv}{dt}\right)dx = m v \, dv$$

Integrate both sides from initial position $x_i$ (velocity $u$) to final position $x_f$ (velocity $v$):

$$W_{\text{net}} = \int_{x_i}^{x_f} F_{\text{net}}\,dx = m \int_{u}^{v} v\,dv = \left[\frac{1}{2}mv^2\right]_u^v = \boxed{\frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{1}{2}mu^2}$$

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Net Work vs Work by a Single Force): $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$ applies strictly to net work (sum of work done by all forces). If a question asks for work done by friction alone, do not equate it to total $\Delta K$ without including gravity and normal forces!

topics.title: Conservative vs. Non-Conservative Forces, Potential Energy Curves & Equilibrium States
topics.theoryHtml:
2.1 Conservative Forces & The Master Relation $F = -\frac{dU}{dx}$
PropertyConservative Forces (Gravity, Spring, Electrostatic)Non-Conservative Forces (Friction, Air Drag, Viscosity)
Work Path DependenceWork done is independent of path; depends only on initial and final positions.Work done depends on the actual path length taken.
Closed Loop WorkWork done in any complete closed round trip is exactly zero ($\oint \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r} = 0$).Work done in a closed loop is negative and non-zero (energy is dissipated as heat).
Force from Potential Energy:
For any conservative force in 1D, force is the negative derivative of potential energy $U(x)$:
$$\boxed{F(x) = -\frac{dU(x)}{dx} \implies \Delta U = U_f - U_i = -\int_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x)\,dx}$$
2.2 Three States of Mechanical Equilibrium
Equilibrium StateCondition on ForceCondition on Potential Energy $U(x)$Physical Stability Behavior
1. Stable Equilibrium$F = -\frac{dU}{dx} = 0$Local Minimum ($\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} > 0$)If displaced slightly, the particle experiences a restoring force pushing it back to equilibrium (like a ball at the bottom of a bowl).
2. Unstable Equilibrium$F = -\frac{dU}{dx} = 0$Local Maximum ($\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} < 0$)If displaced slightly, force pushes it farther away from equilibrium (like a ball balanced on top of a dome).
3. Neutral Equilibrium$F = -\frac{dU}{dx} = 0$Constant / Flat ($\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} = 0$)If displaced, it stays at rest in its new position (like a ball on a flat horizontal table).
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of Spring Potential Energy $U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$:

Spring restoring force is $F_s = -kx$. By definition, $U(x) - U(0) = -\int_0^x (-kx)\,dx = k \int_0^x x\,dx = \boxed{\frac{1}{2}kx^2}$

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Sign Confusion in $F = -dU/dx$): Students often forget the minus sign. If $U(x) = ax^2$, then $F = -2ax$ (acting inward toward the origin, restoring).

topics.title: Conservation of Mechanical Energy & Collision Dynamics (Elastic, Inelastic & Restitution)
topics.theoryHtml:
3.1 Conservation of Mechanical Energy ($E = K + U = \text{Constant}$)
Master Law:
If only conservative forces do work in a system (no friction or air drag), total mechanical energy $E$ remains strictly constant:
$$\boxed{K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f \implies \Delta K + \Delta U = 0}$$
3.2 Coefficient of Restitution ($e$) in Collisions
Collision TypeMomentum ConservationKinetic Energy ConservationCoefficient of Restitution ($e$)
1. Perfectly ElasticYesYes$e = 1$
2. Perfectly InelasticYesNo (Max energy loss, bodies stick together)$e = 0$
3. Partially ElasticYesNo (Partial energy loss)$0 < e < 1$
$$\text{Newton's Experimental Law of Restitution:} \quad \boxed{e = \frac{\text{Relative Speed of Separation}}{\text{Relative Speed of Approach}} = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{u_1 - u_2}}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of Final Velocities in 1D Elastic Collision ($e = 1$):

$$v_1 = \left(\frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right)u_1 + \left(\frac{2m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right)u_2, \qquad v_2 = \left(\frac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\right)u_1 + \left(\frac{m_2 - m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\right)u_2$$

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Energy Conservation in Inelastic Collisions): Total mechanical energy is never conserved in inelastic collisions (some energy converts to heat/sound), but Linear Momentum is ALWAYS conserved in any collision!

topics.title: Vertical Circular Motion: Critical String Tension, Rod Loops & Projectile-Like Circular Exits
topics.theoryHtml:
4.1 Vertical Loop Master Equations & Critical Speeds
Position on LoopTension in String ($T$)Minimum Critical Speed ($v_{\min}$)
Top Point$T_{\top} = \frac{mv_{\top}^2}{r} - mg$$v_{\top} = \sqrt{rg}$ (String just becomes slack, $T=0$)
Bottom Point$T_{\text{bot}} = \frac{mv_{\text{bot}}^2}{r} + mg$$v_{\text{bot}} = \sqrt{5rg}$ (Needed to ensure $v_{\top} = \sqrt{rg}$)
Horizontal Level$T_{\text{mid}} = \frac{mv_{\text{mid}}^2}{r}$$v_{\text{mid}} = \sqrt{3rg}$
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of Bottom Speed $v_{\text{bot}} = \sqrt{5rg}$ using Conservation of Energy:

$$E_{\text{bot}} = E_{\top} \implies \frac{1}{2}m v_{\text{bot}}^2 = \frac{1}{2}m v_{\top}^2 + mg(2r)$$

Substitute $v_{\top} = \sqrt{rg}$: $\frac{1}{2}v_{\text{bot}}^2 = \frac{1}{2}rg + 2rg = \frac{5}{2}rg \implies \boxed{v_{\text{bot}} = \sqrt{5rg}}$
topics.graphSvg: <svg viewBox='0 0 680 190' style='width:100%;max-width:680px;height:auto;'><rect width='680' height='190' rx='8' fill='#080b12' stroke='#1e293b'/><circle cx='340' cy='95' r='60' fill='none' stroke='#00f0ff' stroke-width='2' stroke-dasharray='4,4'/><circle cx='340' cy='35' r='8' fill='#ff0055'/><text x='340' y='20' fill='#ff0055' font-size='12' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle'>Top: v_top = √rg (T = 0)</text><circle cx='340' cy='155' r='8' fill='#00e676'/><text x='340' y='180' fill='#00e676' font-size='12' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle'>Bottom: v_bot = √5rg</text></svg>
topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (String vs. Rod at the Top): If the bob is attached to a rigid light rod instead of a flexible string, it can reach the top with $v = 0$ without collapsing!

conclusion: You have mastered Chapter 05: Work, Energy, Power & Circular Loop! You are now ready to study multi-particle systems and rotation in Chapter 06.

questions.prompt: A force $\vec{F} = (3x^2\hat{i} + 2y\hat{j})\text{ N}$ acts on a particle. Find the work done in moving the particle from origin $(0,0)$ to $(2\text{ m}, 3\text{ m})$ along the path $y = \frac{3}{4}x$.
A ball is dropped from a height $h = 10\text{ m}$ on a hard floor. If the coefficient of restitution is $e = 0.6$, to what height does the ball bounce back after the collision?
questions.explanation: Height after $n$ bounces is $h_n = e^{2n}h_0$. For 1 bounce: $h_1 = (0.6)^2(10) = 0.36 \times 10 = 3.6\text{ m}$.
